On a single VLCC, that’s a ~$50-$58 million potential profit, minus costs (and the risk of getting sunk by Iran, that’s it).

Iran Foreign Ministry spokesperson on the Strait of Hormuz:

"Our negotiations are with Oman, we are focused on reaching an understanding on a route that will ensure safe shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. Our effort is to determine a route at the earliest opportunity, with Oman's consultation and cooperation; a route that will usually be temporary and based on which we can provide shipping in the Strait of Hormuz..."

"So, these are bilateral negotiations between the two coastal states. Others can play a constructive or destructive role in this process, but the issue is with Iran and Oman. What happens next needs to be decided. I also announced last night that an understanding on the safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz is a necessary condition for the opening of Hormuz, but it is not a sufficient condition. The Strait of Hormuz is not closed because of a disagreement between Iran and Oman; Hormuz has been in trouble since March of last year due to the military aggression of the United States and the Zionist regime..."

"As long as America's evil continues, as long as the naval blockade of Iran is declared, as long as America's military aggression against Iran and its interests continues, and as long as all the things that America has violated during this period continue, there will be no significant change in the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, the focus of the negotiations with Oman will be on this issue, and the issues related to Iran and the United States should be examined in the next stages to see in which direction the situation will go..."

"Bagheri," Spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs:

To avoid any ambiguity, it should be stated with whom the negotiations are taking place. We are currently not having negotiations with the United States, and the negotiations with Oman are focused on reaching an agreement regarding the safe passage of ships through the Strait of Hormuz.

The aim is to, in the first opportunity and with the consultation of Oman, determine a route that is, in principle, temporary, and based on which, the safety of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz will be ensured. These are bilateral negotiations between the two coastal states.

Others may certainly appear constructive or destructive, but the matter is related to Iran and Oman. What will happen next needs to be decided.

The Strait of Hormuz was not blocked due to a disagreement between Iran and Oman, but rather due to the actions of the United States, which began last year on March 1st.

As long as the maritime siege and the actions of the United States continue, and as long as all the violations by the United States persist, nothing significant will happen in the situation in the Strait of Hormuz. The focus of the negotiations with Oman will be on the Strait of Hormuz.

The key Saudi export port of Yanbu in the Red Sea appeared to have its busiest day since Houthi threats upended shipping in the region, while more ships transited dark through the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint.

Five very large crude carriers were berthed at Yanbu’s oil-loading terminals on Saturday, according to satellite images, possibly making it the most active day since Iran-backed Houthi rebels imposed a blockade on Saudi ports two weeks ago. The photos were taken by the European Union’s Sentinel 2 satellite, which only flies over the area every few days.
